about: A rate is the probability that one operation of the kind fails so that the bay stops or needs a person; the rates compare layouts under the same assumptions and predict nothing, and each basis is either source (a document we opened) or ours (our own order-of-magnitude judgment).

kinds.what: The transfer cart brings a bare tube in and lowers it into the holder's saddles.
kinds.reasoning: A cart move with a seating step into saddles is a simple fixed-path operation, but a mis-seat needs a person, so about one in a thousand.

kinds.what: The holder closes on the tube.
kinds.reasoning: A pneumatic or electric clamp on a known tube is very repeatable, with sensor or jam faults rarer than a gripper pick.

kinds.what: An arm's gripper takes a part from a rack, pallet or nest.
kinds.reasoning: A known part at a known place with a purpose-built gripper should rarely fail, and about one in a thousand is a judgment; Brightpick reports over 99.7 percent pick success for mixed unknown warehouse items, which is a harder task and not defined as stopping the line, so it was not used.

kinds.what: An arm sets a held part in its place and lets go.
kinds.reasoning: Placing a rail or a 32 kg module onto the tube or rails needs a tolerance fit and a release, so it is judged as hard as a grip.

kinds.what: A nutrunner runs one strap bolt to torque.
kinds.reasoning: Fastening NOK from cross-threading, a wrong seat or a torque fault is judged at a few in a thousand; a research-lab screw pick-and-fasten with a general tool failed 3 of 27 times in the Team O2AS World Robot Summit 2018 paper, which is a far less controlled task and was not used.

kinds.what: The tapered nose pulls a module's hole into line by contact.
kinds.reasoning: Contact alignment depends on module and hole tolerance and can jam, so it is judged a few in a thousand.

kinds.what: One lock pin is inserted into a hole.
kinds.reasoning: Peg-in-hole insertion with a tapered lead-in into a hole the locate step has just lined up works most of the time, and a stuck or missed pin is judged at a few in a thousand.

kinds.what: One pin is swaged or collared.
kinds.reasoning: A swage tool on a seated pin is a well-controlled process, and tool or collar faults are judged at about two in a thousand.

kinds.what: An automatic tool change on a robot flange.
kinds.reasoning: Vendor tool changers are rated for hundreds of thousands of cycles, but misalignment or air and signal faults still happen, so about one in a thousand.

kinds.what: The holder releases the finished bay.
kinds.reasoning: The same device as clamp, with a small added risk of sticking on the finished bay.

kinds.what: The cart lifts the bay and takes it out.
kinds.reasoning: Same kind of cart operation as tube_in, with a heavier load.

kinds.what: One planned, collision-free move of an arm between poses, as a protective stop or fault risk.
kinds.reasoning: Maker MTBF claims of 40,000 to 100,000 hours (The Robot Report, 2019) cover hardware failure only and would give about 1e-7 per move at a few hundred moves per hour, so we set 1e-4, which is about 1.7 percent per bay at 170 moves, to allow for protective stops and faults that a person must clear.

kinds.what: A part passed directly from one arm to another.
kinds.reasoning: Arm-to-arm transfer needs two arms to agree on a part at the same time, so it is judged riskier than a grip, and it is unused today.
